items.question: A B2B SaaS vendor's Claude-based support-ticket classifier lets each of 700 tenants append custom instructions to a shared base prompt. The vendor wants to change the base prompt to improve category precision. The evaluation suite exercises the base prompt alone, with no tenant instructions attached. What should the vendor do before shipping?

options.A: Evaluate the new base against a volume-stratified sample of real tenant instruction sets, then roll out by tenant cohort against a quality threshold.
options.B: Ship to all tenants at once, since the base prompt is the vendor's to change under the terms of service, and tenant instructions are appended after it rather than mixed into it.
options.C: Ask all 700 tenants to re-test their own instruction sets in a sandbox and confirm acceptance before the change is applied to their environment.
options.D: Freeze tenant custom instructions for the duration of the change so the variable is eliminated, then unfreeze once the new base is stable.

items.question: A run team has been given responsibility for a production Claude system. What must accompany that responsibility for the arrangement to work at three in the morning?

options.A: A documented service level agreement with each business unit that consumes the system's output.
options.B: Authority to roll back the prompt and model version and to disable the feature, without seeking the build team's approval.
options.C: A dedicated budget line covering the system's inference spend and the supporting infrastructure, owned by the run team's own cost centre.
options.D: Read access to the source repository, the prompt registry and the latest evaluation results.

items.question: A utility's run team is four weeks into an eight-week shadowing handover of a Claude-based outage-notification drafter, with the build team still on call as backup. At 21:40 the drafter begins producing customer messages that name the wrong substations. The runbook's rollback is a single command. The run-team engineer on shift has never executed a rollback in production and this step has not yet been drilled. The build team's on-call engineer answers the phone immediately. What is the next step?

options.A: The build-team engineer performs the rollback, since customer-facing messages are already wrong and the run-team engineer has never run the procedure.
options.B: The run-team engineer escalates to the product owner to confirm that incorrect substation names justify a rollback before anything is changed.
options.C: The build-team engineer stays on the line while the run-team engineer executes the rollback, and the undrilled step goes to the handover review.
options.D: The run-team engineer disables the drafter entirely and leaves the rollback for the build team to perform during business hours tomorrow.

items.question: After migrating a production system from one pinned model version to its successor, why must monitoring baselines be re-established?

options.A: Because the metrics recorded against the previous version are discarded when the pin is changed.
options.B: Because alert thresholds are stored against the model version identifier in the monitoring configuration and do not carry across a version migration.
options.C: Because the successor's rate limits differ, which changes the shape of the observed error-rate series.
options.D: Because thresholds tuned to the old version's output distribution will either fire constantly or stop firing, and both leave you blind.

items.question: A contact centre with 45% annual agent turnover rolled out a Claude-based response assistant to 600 agents through a one-off classroom programme delivered over six weeks. Six months later, quality audit scores among agents hired since the programme are materially below those of agents who attended it. Which two changes address the cause? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Repeat the six-week classroom programme once a year, so that every cohort of joiners eventually receives the same full training the original population did.
options.B: Fold the assistant module into the standard new-hire induction curriculum, owned by the training function rather than the project team.
options.C: Require team leaders to attest that each new joiner has read the assistant guidance before taking live calls.
options.D: Embed the key checks as in-product guidance at the moment the agent reviews the assistant's output.
options.E: Publish the training deck on the intranet and email the link to each new joiner on their first day.

items.question: A platform team is shipping a prompt change to a shared Claude-based service consumed by several downstream teams. Beyond stating that behaviour has changed, what should the release note tell those teams?

options.A: Which output characteristics changed, on which input classes, and what each consuming team should re-test.
options.B: The full text of the previous and new prompts, so that consuming teams can diff them and reach their own conclusions.
options.C: The evaluation scores before and after the change, so teams can judge for themselves whether it was an improvement.
options.D: The rationale for the change and the stakeholder who requested it, so teams know where to direct questions.

items.question: A charity's Claude-based donor-correspondence drafter has been through eight iterations in ten months. Each of the last three raised the internal quality score by under one point on a 100-point scale, while the team's own estimate of sampling noise on that score is about two points. Volunteers who use the drafter daily report no perceptible difference across those three releases. The product owner has asked for a ninth iteration on the same axis. What should the architect advise?

options.A: Continue, since small gains compound over time and the score remains well below the maximum the scale allows.
options.B: Increase the evaluation sample size until sub-point improvements can be resolved reliably, then resume iterating on the same axis.
options.C: Stop iterating on this axis, because the measured gains sit inside the instrument's noise, and move the effort to an axis where a difference would be observable.
options.D: Replace the internal quality score with a model-graded rubric that is more sensitive to small differences between releases.

items.question: What is the primary purpose of a superuser or champion network during the rollout of an AI assistant?

options.A: To reduce the training budget by delegating formal instruction to volunteers instead of professional trainers.
options.B: To place a credible local source of help, and of realistic expectations, next to each user group.
options.C: To give the programme team a controlled group on which to test new prompt versions before wider release.
options.D: To create a governance forum with authority to approve changes to the assistant's behaviour.

items.question: A city transport authority's contract with its systems integrator specifies one acceptance milestone for a Claude-based journey-disruption assistant: accepted or not on a single date following a two-week user acceptance test, with payment tied to that milestone. The architect wants phased delivery to limit exposure. The contract cannot be reopened this financial year. What should the architect do?

options.A: Deliver internally in phases and present only the final phase as the contractual acceptance deliverable, keeping the milestone untouched.
options.B: Accept the single milestone and mitigate by extending user acceptance testing from two weeks to six with a broader tester population.
options.C: Ask the authority to waive acceptance for the first release and take the system provisionally while phasing is arranged informally.
options.D: Keep the milestone and phase technically inside it: ship behind a flag, enable progressively by user group against pre-agreed criteria, with a rollback the authority controls.

items.question: A retailer is retiring its in-house Claude-based product-description generator after two years and moving to a vendor SaaS product. The team is preparing to archive the repository and shut the service down. Which two assets should be preserved and transferred to the team adopting the vendor product? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: The evaluation set and rubric built from two years of production failures, the only instrument that can test whether the vendor product is at least as good.
options.B: The prompt library, so the incoming team can paste the same instructions into the vendor product's configuration screens rather than rewrite them for its own controls.
options.C: The complete conversation logs of every generation request served over the two years of operation, exported to the retailer's archive.
options.D: The catalogue of known failure modes and product categories where output was consistently weak, so the vendor product is tested against them before cutover.
options.E: The infrastructure-as-code definitions and deployment pipelines that built and released the retiring generator service.

items.question: In the composable-patterns view of Claude system design, what distinguishes the augmented LLM baseline from every workflow pattern built on top of it?

options.A: It is pinned to the cheapest available tier, because higher tiers are reserved for the individual steps of a workflow.
options.B: It runs without a system prompt, because role and output-format instructions first appear in a workflow's step prompts.
options.C: It performs no tool calls, because handing the model a search or code-execution tool is what makes a system agentic.
options.D: It is a single model invocation that may use retrieval, tools and memory, with no orchestration code around the call.

items.question: A freight forwarder generates customs declarations from scanned commercial invoices using one Claude call that extracts line items, assigns each an HS tariff code, and emits the declaration XML. A post-launch audit finds that 6% of declarations carry a plausible-looking HS code that does not exist in the current tariff file; each one triggers a manual broker correction costing about £40. Extraction itself audits clean. The per-declaration latency budget is 20 seconds and the system currently runs at 4. Which change best addresses the defect?

options.A: Move the whole call to the Opus tier and add an explicit system-prompt rule never to emit a tariff code that is not currently valid.
options.B: Run three parallel calls with differently worded classification prompts and take the majority HS code per line item before emitting the XML.
options.C: Keep the single call but paste the full current tariff schedule into the system prompt, so the model can only choose codes that appear in it.
options.D: Split into an extract-then-classify chain, with a deterministic tariff-file lookup between classification and XML generation that returns failed codes for retry.

items.question: A telco handles 90,000 inbound support conversations a day. A Haiku router classifies each opening message into one of five intents; 'billing dispute' and 'service outage' dispatch to Opus-backed pipelines, the rest to Haiku pipelines. Offline the router is 94% accurate. In production, satisfaction collapsed for one segment: customers reporting outages who were classified as 'general enquiry' received a scripted troubleshooting reply and churned. Misrouting a general enquiry into the outage pipeline costs roughly four times the tokens and causes no customer harm. What is the right adjustment?

options.A: Use the router's per-class confidence to send any conversation carrying a plausible outage or dispute signal to the Opus pipeline.
options.B: Retrain the router on 50,000 newly labelled conversations until offline accuracy exceeds 98%, then leave the dispatch logic unchanged.
options.C: Remove the router and send all 90,000 daily conversations to the Opus-backed pipeline, so a misroute becomes impossible.
options.D: Keep the router and have the general-enquiry pipeline detect outage language mid-conversation and hand off to the Opus pipeline.

items.question: An energy utility is automating fault diagnosis for distribution transformers. Engineers propose an agent that queries SCADA history, pulls maintenance records, requests additional telemetry and iterates until it converges on a root cause — typically 8 to 20 tool calls. On 300 historical faults the agent reaches the correct root cause 71% of the time; a fixed three-step workflow (retrieve telemetry window, summarise anomalies, classify against the fault taxonomy) reaches 68%. The agent costs nine times the tokens and takes forty times as long. The architect blocks the agent. What is the strongest architectural justification?

options.A: Agentic designs are inappropriate for regulated infrastructure, because a run whose step count cannot be predicted cannot pass change control.
options.B: Fault diagnosis is fundamentally a classification task against the fault taxonomy, so it belongs in a fixed workflow rather than an autonomous loop.
options.C: The agent's 8 to 20 tool calls will exhaust the context window on transformers with decades of SCADA history, leaving the workflow as the only option.
options.D: Every tool returns more evidence and none returns a verdict, so the loop has no environment signal to correct its hypothesis against.

items.question: A games publisher localises in-game dialogue from English into nine languages with Claude. A reviewer proposes an evaluator–optimiser loop: a generator produces the translation, a separate evaluator critiques it against the style guide, and the generator revises, up to three rounds. Which conditions would genuinely justify the loop rather than a single well-engineered generation call? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: The publisher wants to cut the per-line token cost of localising a 40,000-line dialogue pack before the next release.
options.B: Reviewers can articulate the criteria they apply — character voice, glossary adherence, UI line limits — precisely enough to write a rubric.
options.C: The nine target languages can be generated concurrently, cutting wall-clock time for a full pack to that of one language.
options.D: A held-out sample shows measurable quality improvement between the generator's first draft and its revised output.
options.E: The generator occasionally returns output that fails the game engine's dialogue import schema and blocks the nightly build.

items.question: A hospital network drafts discharge summaries with a four-step prompt chain: extract encounter facts, draft the summary, check against a required-sections checklist, apply a readability rewrite. The rewrite step was added last sprint to satisfy a plain-language obligation that goes live next month. Since then clinician edit rate has risen from 22% to 34%, and two summaries were found to have lost a medication change that the draft step had captured correctly. Every step's input and output is logged. What should the team do next?

options.A: Add a fifth step that compares the rewritten summary against the draft and reinstates any medication change the rewrite dropped.
options.B: Replace the chain with a single call that drafts the summary, applies the section checklist and meets the reading-level target in one pass.
options.C: Remove the readability rewrite step and revert to the three-step chain, restoring the 22% edit rate until the obligation lands.
options.D: Diff the logged draft-step output against the rewrite-step output on the affected summaries, then measure how often content is lost.

items.question: Parallelisation appears in two forms in the standard pattern vocabulary. What distinguishes sectioning from voting?

options.A: Sectioning assigns each subtask its own model tier, while voting runs every attempt on one tier so the results stay comparable.
options.B: Sectioning aggregates its results by majority vote, while voting stitches its attempts together by concatenation.
options.C: Sectioning is executed synchronously on the request path, while voting is dispatched asynchronously and collected later.
options.D: Sectioning splits a task into independent subtasks that are merged; voting repeats one task and aggregates the attempts.

items.question: An investigative newsroom builds a research tool over a leaked set of 40,000 documents. For a question such as 'how much did Company X pay Contractor Y between 2019 and 2021', the system must decide which document families to open, and that decision depends on what the first documents reveal — a payment ledger may name three subsidiaries nobody knew existed. The current design fans out a fixed set of six parallel calls (contracts, invoices, emails, board minutes, filings, press) and merges their answers. Recall on multi-hop questions is poor. Which pattern change addresses the root cause?

options.A: Put an orchestrator in front that decides at runtime which searches to task workers with and spawns follow-ups as findings emerge.
options.B: Chain the six calls sequentially so each worker sees the findings of the one before it and can refine its own search.
options.C: Increase the fixed fan-out from six parallel calls to twelve, adding families such as bank statements, shipping records and court filings.
options.D: Add an evaluator–optimiser loop that scores the merged answer for completeness and returns it to the merger for another attempt.

items.question: A national benefits agency is automating first-pass eligibility assessment for a disability payment. Statute requires that for any decision the agency can produce the exact evidence considered and the order in which the statutory criteria were applied, and that an appeals officer can reproduce the assessment two years later. The delivery team's prototype is an agent that chooses which evidence to pull and when to stop, and it performs well on historical cases. What is the correct architectural response?

options.A: Implement the statutory criteria as an explicit workflow — one step per criterion in the mandated order — and persist every step's inputs and outputs.
options.B: Keep the agent and log the full trajectory — every tool call, its arguments and its result — so an appeals officer can replay the run.
options.C: Keep the agent but pin the model version and set temperature to zero, so that identical inputs produce an identical trajectory.
options.D: Keep the agent for the assessment and add a second Claude call that writes the criterion-by-criterion narrative for the appeals file.

items.question: An agritech startup is scoping a feature that turns a farmer's free-text field note plus the farm's sensor history into a spray recommendation. The lead engineer's design document opens with a five-step chain, an intent router and an evaluator loop. The product has no users, no production traffic and no labelled examples. The CTO pushes back on the design. What should the team build first?

options.A: The router, since the intent taxonomy constrains everything downstream and is cheapest to fix before other components depend on it.
options.B: The evaluator loop, since until a critic scores each recommendation the team has no way to tell whether anything else works.
options.C: The full five-step chain, instrumented per step, then delete whichever steps later measurement shows add nothing to quality.
options.D: A single augmented call with retrieval over sensor history and the agronomy reference, measured on hand-labelled field notes.

items.question: A video platform screens 500,000 user comments an hour for a narrow category of prohibited content. A single Haiku call catches 88% of true violations with a 0.4% false-positive rate, sending roughly 2,000 comments an hour to human review. Legal exposure from a missed violation is severe; the human review vendor is contracted to handle up to 12,000 items an hour. The team now runs three differently-prompted calls per comment. How should the votes be combined?

options.A: Flag when at least two of the three agree, holding review volume near today's 2,000 an hour while lifting recall a little.
options.B: Drop the ensemble and run a single Sonnet call per comment, funded by the tokens the three Haiku calls were spending.
options.C: Flag only when all three calls agree, and send the disagreements to a Sonnet call for a tie-breaking second opinion.
options.D: Flag when any one of the three calls flags, taking review volume to about 6,000 an hour against the contracted ceiling.

items.question: An architecture review board is choosing between a fixed workflow and an agentic loop for a new automation. Which properties of the task argue for the workflow? (Choose THREE.)

options.A: The steps required are known in advance and do not vary from one input to the next.
options.B: The task requires a dozen or more tool calls against internal systems per request.
options.C: Each step writes to a system where mistakes cannot be reversed, so every transition needs a check.
options.D: The team would rather not write and maintain the orchestration code a fixed path requires.
options.E: The response must complete inside a tight and predictable latency budget on every request.

items.question: An online grocery retailer routes customer messages with a lightweight classifier: simple ones (order status, delivery window) go to Haiku, complex ones (refund disputes, allergy queries) go to Sonnet. Average cost per message falls 60%. Which risk does this design introduce that the previous single-model design did not have?

options.A: A complex message classified as simple gets the weaker configuration, and nothing downstream detects it.
options.B: Maintaining two prompt sets and two regression suites becomes the dominant new cost of the design.
options.C: Haiku and Sonnet return different output shapes, so the reply templating layer must parse two formats.
options.D: Total token spend rises, because the classifier call is added to every message on top of the answer call.

items.question: A law firm's contract-redlining assistant runs a generator–critic loop: Claude proposes redlines against the firm's playbook, a critic call assesses them, and the generator revises. The loop is implemented as one conversation — the critic turn is appended to the same message list that contains the generator's reasoning and drafts. Partners report that the critic almost always finds the redlines acceptable and that output quality is no better than a single pass. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: The critic shares a thread containing the generator's own reasoning and anchors on it; an independent evaluator needs its own call.
options.B: Two revision rounds is too few for a generator–critic loop to converge; playbook redlining typically needs five or more.
options.C: The playbook is long enough that it is silently truncated once the full contract is appended alongside it in the prompt.
options.D: The critic is running on the same tier as the generator, when a critic should sit one tier below so that it is less inclined to defer.

items.question: A pharmaceutical company drafts regulatory submission sections with Claude, one call per section. QA rejects about one in five drafts. Root-cause review shows rejections cluster on three things: a cited study that does not appear in the company's study register, a numeric endpoint that disagrees with the statistical report, and tone a reviewer describes as promotional. The team has decided to decompose the single call. Which decomposition delivers the most value?

options.A: Split by the section's subheadings, generating each subsection in its own call and concatenating the results in template order.
options.B: Split along the three failure modes — citations against the study register, figures against the statistical report, tone against a rubric.
options.C: Keep the single call and wrap it in an evaluator–optimiser loop that critiques the draft against one combined QA rubric until it passes.
options.D: Split into a plan-then-write chain: one call outlines the section against the regulatory template, a second turns the outline into prose.

items.question: Prompt chaining decomposes a task into a fixed sequence of model calls, each handling one subtask. What trade does the pattern make?

options.A: It trades accuracy for latency: the steps finish sooner, but each one is individually less reliable than a single call.
options.B: It trades cost for determinism: total tokens fall because each call carries a shorter prompt and a narrower instruction set.
options.C: It trades latency for accuracy: each call gets an easier job, paid for with extra round trips and repeated context.
options.D: It trades context for tool access: each chained step can be given tools that a single augmented call cannot reach.

items.question: A recruiting platform shipped an agentic candidate-sourcing feature behind a flag serving 4% of accounts. The agent searches, opens profiles and refines its query until it has ten matches; it reaches ten matches on 82% of runs against 61% for the fixed sourcing workflow it replaced, and costs six times as much per run. Recruiters accept 2.1 candidates per agent run and 1.9 per workflow run. The product manager wants to roll out to everyone. What should the team do next?

options.A: Widen the flag to 25% of accounts to tighten the confidence interval on the agent's match rate before deciding.
options.B: Keep both implementations and route by account tier, giving enterprise accounts the agent and self-serve the fixed workflow.
options.C: Cut the agent's cost by moving its profile-reading steps to Haiku, then re-measure the match rate at the new price point.
options.D: Run a head-to-head at enough volume to resolve the difference in accepted candidates per run before deciding on rollout.

items.question: An airline's disruption assistant must, for each stranded passenger, (1) summarise the itinerary and entitlements, (2) draft a rebooking rationale, (3) screen the draft for tone and required regulatory language, and (4) compute a compensation figure from the fare rules. Steps 2 and 3 run sequentially after 1; step 4 depends only on the booking record and fare rules. The p95 budget for the whole response is 6 seconds and the pipeline currently runs at 7.4. Which changes correctly exploit parallelisation here? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Run step 3 concurrently with step 2, giving the screener step 1's summary rather than waiting for step 2's draft.
options.B: Run step 4 concurrently with the 1-2-3 sequence, since it depends only on the fare rules and the booking record.
options.C: Run three copies of step 2 concurrently with differently worded prompts and take the majority rebooking rationale.
options.D: Move steps 2 and 3 to the Batch API so their tokens and time no longer count against the interactive p95 budget.
options.E: Split step 1 into two concurrent calls, one for the itinerary and one for entitlements, merging before step 2.

items.question: Routing classifies an input and dispatches it to a specialised downstream handler. What condition must hold for routing to improve a system rather than degrade it?

options.A: The categories must be few enough — four or five at most — that one well-written prompt could have covered them all anyway.
options.B: Inputs fall into categories that are better handled separately, and classification is accurate enough to get them there.
options.C: Every downstream path must run on the same model tier, so that routing changes the cost profile without changing quality.
options.D: The router must see the full conversation history rather than a single message, because message-level classification is unreliable.

items.question: A logistics operator answers dispatcher questions about a 1,200-vehicle fleet, such as 'which of tomorrow's northbound loads are at risk?'. Questions vary widely and only some need driver-hours or weather data, so an orchestrator plans which workers to dispatch; each worker queries one system (telematics, driver hours, weather, customer SLAs) and returns a prose summary. p95 is 22 seconds against a 10-second target. Instrumentation shows the workers run concurrently and take about 5 seconds, retrieval and network account for about 4, the planning call about 3, and the final synthesis call about 10 because its prompt carries every worker's full summary. What is the most effective change?

options.A: Replace the orchestrator with a fixed parallel fan-out to all four systems on every question, which removes the planning call.
options.B: Move the four worker calls to Haiku so that each system query returns faster and the concurrent stage shortens.
options.C: Have workers return compact structured records rather than prose summaries, so the synthesis call reads and writes far less.
options.D: Run the synthesis call on Opus so that it digests the four worker summaries more accurately and emits fewer output tokens.

items.question: A construction contractor processes requests for information (RFIs) on large projects. The end-to-end process is fixed by the main contract: log the RFI, classify it against the contract's response-time tiers, gather the relevant drawings and specifications, draft a response, route it to the responsible discipline lead for sign-off, and issue it. Only the gathering stage is unpredictable — one RFI may need a single drawing while another needs a dozen documents across revisions, and which ones are needed depends on what earlier documents cross-reference. Where should autonomy sit in this design?

options.A: Keep the process as a workflow and make only the gathering stage a bounded agentic loop, handing its evidence set to the next fixed step.
options.B: Make the whole process an agent, since one stage already requires autonomy and mixing paradigms doubles the maintenance surface.
options.C: Keep the process a workflow and handle gathering with a fixed parallel fan-out across the drawing, specification and revision-history repositories.
options.D: Keep the process a workflow and leave gathering to a human, since the variability of that stage makes it unsuitable for automation.

items.question: Both a prompt chain with a validation gate and an evaluator–optimiser loop can send an output back for another attempt. What is the substantive difference between them?

options.A: The gate retries against the same model, whereas the loop escalates each successive retry to a higher capability tier.
options.B: A gate's retries can be issued in parallel across candidates, whereas an evaluator–optimiser loop is necessarily serial.
options.C: A gate is applied once at the end of the chain, whereas the loop's evaluator runs after every step in the pipeline it wraps.
options.D: A gate applies a programmatic pass/fail test at a fixed point; the loop uses model judgement and iterates to a limit.

items.question: A public transport authority serves its rider assistant from a single Claude prompt. The team proposes splitting it into a router plus four specialised handlers. Which production observations would justify that change? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: The single prompt has grown past 4,000 words, and reviewers now struggle to tell which instruction governs a given answer type.
options.B: Overall answer accuracy is 91% against the team's 95% target, with no single intent standing out in the error breakdown.
options.C: Instructions added to improve timetable answers measurably degraded accessibility answers, and the reverse held as well.
options.D: Peak-hour traffic runs at three times off-peak volume, and the team wants to smooth the load across its rate limits.
options.E: Two of the four intents are answerable from a structured timetable API and never need retrieval, while the others always do.

items.question: A clinical coding vendor assigns diagnosis codes from physician notes. To raise confidence it runs the same prompt three times at non-zero temperature and accepts a code only on unanimous agreement. Audit finds the unanimous outputs are wrong on the same 4% of notes the single call was wrong on before — almost all cases where the physician's shorthand is ambiguous between two codes and the model consistently selects the more common one. Coder review load has not fallen. What does this tell the architect?

options.A: Three samples is too few; nine samples at the same temperature would surface the minority code often enough to break unanimity.
options.B: Repeated sampling of one prompt cannot detect an error the prompt itself causes; these notes need diversity or an explicit disambiguation step.
options.C: Unanimity is the wrong aggregation rule here; majority voting would surface the minority code and flag the note for coder review.
options.D: Temperature should be reduced to zero, since non-zero sampling is what lets the ensemble drift onto the wrong code at all.

items.question: A food manufacturer produces label-compliance reports with parallel sectioning: five concurrent calls each assess one regulatory area (allergens, nutrition claims, origin labelling, additives, packaging) over the same product dossier, and a sixth call merges them into one report. QA has found reports where the allergen section states that a 'may contain' warning is required while the packaging section states the current label is compliant. The merge call produced readable prose and flagged nothing. What should the team do next?

options.A: Re-run the five section assessments on Opus, so that their verdicts agree with one another more often across the dossier.
options.B: Chain the five sections sequentially in regulatory order so each one can see the findings of the sections before it.
options.C: Have each section emit a structured verdict with severity and cited clause, and have the merge apply a precedence rule for conflicts.
options.D: Add an evaluator–optimiser loop over the merged report that critiques it for internal consistency and sends it back for revision until it passes.

items.question: Compared with a fixed workflow performing the same task, where does the bulk of an agentic loop's additional token cost come from?

options.A: Re-sending an accumulating context on every iteration, so consumption grows with the number of steps a run takes.
options.B: The higher per-token price of the Opus-class tiers that agentic designs require in order to plan their next step reliably.
options.C: The orchestration code needed to manage the loop, its retries and its stopping rule, which dwarfs a workflow's.
options.D: The trajectory evaluation and monitoring infrastructure agents need, which is where most of the incremental spend lands.

items.question: A university admissions office summarises applicant files with a single Claude call that reads transcripts, personal statements and references and produces a structured reviewer brief. Reviewers say the briefs are broadly good, but grade conversions from international transcripts are wrong often enough that they re-check every one, which erases the time saved. The office has 3,000 historical files with reviewer-corrected briefs. Which changes would let the team target the failing part specifically? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Split grade conversion into its own step so it can be prompted, evaluated and gated independently of the narrative summary.
options.B: Move the whole call to the Opus tier and re-measure whether reviewers regain trust in the briefs they are given.
options.C: Add an evaluator–optimiser loop over the whole brief, with a rubric derived from the 3,000 reviewer corrections.
options.D: Build an eval set from the 3,000 corrected briefs, restricted to the grade-conversion fields so that step can be measured alone.
options.E: Ask reviewers to stop re-checking conversions and to flag errors after the fact instead, so the time saving is realised now.

items.question: A third-party logistics provider wants Claude to resolve inventory discrepancies in its warehouse management system. The proposed agent inspects scan history, cycle-count records and order data, then writes an adjustment directly to the WMS. Adjustments propagate within seconds to customer-facing stock levels and to the billing engine, and there is no bulk undo — reversing one requires a manual counter-adjustment plus a credit note. In a shadow run the agent resolved 84% of discrepancies correctly. What is the right design?

options.A: Deploy the agent with write access and monitor the daily adjustment error rate, reversing any wrong adjustment once it is detected.
options.B: Deploy the agent with write access but restrict it to one low-volume warehouse until its measured accuracy exceeds 95%.
options.C: Abandon the agentic design and implement a fixed workflow that assembles the evidence and flags every discrepancy for human resolution.
options.D: Let the agent investigate freely but emit a proposed adjustment with evidence, gating the write behind a value and confidence policy.

items.question: A meal-kit company generates recipe cards from chefs' rough notes. The original implementation was one call. Over eighteen months it grew into an eleven-step chain: normalise units, extract ingredients, order the method, estimate times, write the introduction, check allergens, adjust for portion count, apply house style, generate the shopping list, check reading level, format. Median latency is 31 seconds against a 20-second target, nobody currently on the team can say what four of the steps are for, and quality on the team's eval set is three points better than the original single call. What should the architect propose?

options.A: Keep all eleven steps but run the mutually independent ones concurrently to bring median latency inside the 20-second target.
options.B: Ablate each step against the eval set, keep those that move the score or enforce a check, and fold the rest into neighbours.
options.C: Revert to the original single call, since three points of quality do not justify eleven steps and 31 seconds of latency.
options.D: Rewrite the pipeline as an agent so the model decides which of the eleven operations a given chef's note actually needs.

items.question: A team is considering replacing a fixed workflow with an agentic loop. Which production observations genuinely support that change? (Choose THREE.)

options.A: Per-request cost has climbed steadily as the workflow's prompts and few-shot examples have grown longer.
options.B: A growing share of requests need steps in an order the workflow lacks, and the team keeps adding conditional branches.
options.C: The available tools return outcomes the model can act on, such as a query returning no rows or a validation failing.
options.D: The individual steps are accurate, but the final synthesis step produces output reviewers call weak and unfocused.
options.E: The number of steps a request needs varies widely and cannot be predicted from the request itself.

items.question: In a routing design, when should a deterministic rule-based router be preferred to a model-based classifier?

options.A: Whenever there are four or fewer destinations, since a classifier only earns its extra call and latency above that.
options.B: Whenever the routing call would consume more than a tenth of the end-to-end latency budget for the request.
options.C: When the routing signal is already present in structured metadata or an unambiguous surface feature of the request.
options.D: When the destinations run on different model tiers, since a classifier cannot be trusted to make cost-affecting decisions.

items.question: A brand agency ships a Claude tool that drafts campaign taglines. It uses an evaluator–optimiser loop: generate ten taglines, critique them against 'brand fit and memorability', regenerate, repeat for three rounds. Creative directors report that the final round is consistently blander than the first and have started asking engineers for the round-one output. The rubric given to the critic each round is the same one-line brief. What is the correct read?

options.A: The criteria are too vague to critique against, so each round pushes toward safer language; make the rubric checkable or drop the loop.
options.B: Three rounds is too many for creative work; a single critique round would remove the weak taglines while preserving the distinctive ones.
options.C: The critic needs few-shot examples of taglines the agency considers strong, which would let it judge memorability reliably enough for the loop.
options.D: The generator and the critic should run on different model tiers — Opus generating, Sonnet critiquing — so the critique is not self-referential.

items.question: What does a team pay when it decomposes a task into more steps than the task actually needs?

options.A: Lower accuracy at each step, because a model given a narrow instruction performs worse than one given the whole task at once.
options.B: The ability to run steps concurrently, since a longer chain necessarily contains more dependencies between its steps.
options.C: Output diversity, because each additional step constrains the range of responses the pipeline is able to produce.
options.D: Serial latency and re-sent context at every hop, plus more prompts to version, monitor and debug for no added check.

items.question: A children's learning app sends every pupil message to Claude for a tutoring reply, and must also screen each message for safeguarding concerns. The product manager proposes folding the safeguarding instructions into the tutoring system prompt so that one call does both. The app has a two-second response target. What is the better design?

options.A: Fold the safeguarding instructions into the tutoring prompt as proposed, since one call is cheaper and avoids a second round trip.
options.B: Chain a safeguarding check after the tutoring call so the screen assesses the reply, blocking it before delivery if it fails.
options.C: Run the safeguarding classifier as a concurrent call with its own prompt, thresholds and eval set, so it stays independent.
options.D: Route on a safeguarding keyword list, so matches go to a screening pipeline and everything else goes straight to tutoring.

items.question: An online travel agency is reviewing an agent that handles 'change my booking' requests. The agent currently makes all of the decisions below on its own. Which should be moved out of the model's discretion and into deterministic code? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Which of the traveller's three current bookings an ambiguously worded request refers to.
options.B: Whether the fare rules permit the requested change, and what change fee and fare difference apply.
options.C: How to word the confirmation message sent to the traveller once the change has been made.
options.D: Whether the requesting party is authorised to modify the booking they name.
options.E: Which airline policy documents to retrieve before formulating an answer for the traveller.

items.question: A mining group's COO has asked for 'an agent' to handle purchase-requisition approvals, after reading a competitor's press release. The process is fully specified in the group's delegation-of-authority matrix: value bands, category rules and a fixed escalation ladder. The only judgement in it is deciding whether a free-text justification adequately supports the requested category, which a single Claude call does well in testing. The architect must respond this week. What should the architect do next?

options.A: Map the process against the delegation-of-authority matrix, show that only the justification needs judgement, and propose a one-call workflow.
options.B: Build a small agent prototype this week so the COO can see it working, then compare it with a workflow at the next review.
options.C: Explain that agentic designs are unsuitable for regulated approval processes such as this one, and propose the workflow instead.
options.D: Build the workflow and describe it to the COO as an agent, since the distinction is internal engineering terminology anyway.

items.question: An insurer's subrogation team recovers costs from third parties. An engineer proposes replacing the current two-call design — extract a structured liability summary from the claim file, then draft the demand letter — with a single call that reads the file and writes the letter, saving about 40% of tokens and 1.8 seconds per case. Today the liability summary is reviewed and edited by a recovery specialist before the letter is generated, and about 15% of summaries are corrected. Should the team merge the calls?

options.A: Yes: the token and latency savings are real, and the specialist can review the finished letter instead, which is the artefact that actually leaves the building.
options.B: No: the summary is the review point 15% of cases depend on, and merging removes the only place to correct the facts before drafting.
options.C: No: a single call cannot reliably produce a structured liability summary and persuasive prose in one response, so the merged design fails on format.
options.D: Yes, provided the merged call runs on a higher capability tier, which would reduce the correction rate enough to make the review point unnecessary.

items.question: A car manufacturer's in-car assistant must answer within 900ms p95 from end of speech. The pipeline is a Haiku router (about 180ms) that classifies the utterance into one of six intents, then a handler call (about 600ms). Adding owner's-manual retrieval, which takes about 270ms and runs after routing, pushed p95 to about 1,050ms. Navigation and climate intents are answerable from vehicle state alone; the other four need the manual. Retrieval must not be dropped. What is the strongest change?

options.A: Merge routing into the handler so one call both classifies and answers, requesting the manual through a tool call when it needs it.
options.B: Match navigation and climate utterances against a keyword list so those two intents skip the router and its 180ms.
options.C: Move the handler to a faster tier on the four manual-backed intents, recovering roughly the 270ms that retrieval added.
options.D: Issue the manual retrieval speculatively alongside the router, discarding the result for intents that do not need it.

items.question: In parallel sectioning, what determines the pattern's end-to-end latency?

options.A: The duration of the slowest section plus the aggregation step, so one slow section sets the floor for the stage.
options.B: The mean duration of the sections plus the aggregation step, since running them concurrently averages their durations.
options.C: The sum of the sections' durations, reduced by whatever concurrency the client library manages to achieve in practice.
options.D: The aggregation step alone, because the sections complete while the aggregator is still assembling its own prompt.

items.question: An enterprise software vendor's support team triages customer log bundles. An engineer opens a bundle, searches for candidate errors, follows whichever thread looks promising, pulls the customer's configuration, sometimes re-runs a query against the customer's schema, and stops once a cause can be named. Bundles range from 3MB to 4GB. The team proposes an agent. Which facts in this situation genuinely support the agentic design? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: The bundles are far larger than any context window, so whatever is built must be organised around retrieval rather than around reading the whole artefact.
options.B: Which artefact to open next depends on what the previous one contained, and the number of hops varies substantially from one bundle to the next.
options.C: A support engineer's hour costs considerably more than the tokens an agent would consume working through one log bundle.
options.D: The team already maintains a documented triage runbook covering the eight most common failure classes and their fixes.
options.E: Tools return checkable outcomes — no matches, a missing configuration key, a query that errors — so the model can tell if a step advanced.

items.question: A national statistics office generates plain-English descriptions of dataset variables. An evaluator–optimiser loop critiques each description against a published style standard and regenerates until the critique passes. In the first month, 0.3% of variables never passed: the loop ran the team's configured maximum of ten rounds, and for eleven variables the pipeline emitted nothing at all, because the code only wrote output on a passing critique. Each non-passing variable consumed twenty model calls. What should the design do instead?

options.A: Raise the round limit from ten to twenty-five so that slow-converging variables eventually reach a passing critique.
options.B: Pre-classify the variables likely to be difficult and route those straight to a human writer, keeping the loop for the rest.
options.C: Lower the round cap and, on exhaustion, emit the best candidate so far flagged for review rather than nothing.
options.D: Have the evaluator relax its threshold after the fifth round, so that every variable terminates with a pass.

items.question: A plumbing franchise's dispatcher tool answers questions such as 'who can reach the Kettering job before 3pm?'. The proposed design is a four-step chain: parse the question, fetch engineer locations, fetch the job schedule, compose an answer. Another engineer objects that this should be one call with two tools. Traffic is about 400 questions a day, both data sources are simple lookups, and the answer is displayed to a human dispatcher who can rephrase and ask again. Who is right?

options.A: The objector: with two simple lookups and a human reading the result, none of the chain's boundaries carries a check.
options.B: The original design: parsing in a dedicated step makes the downstream steps materially more reliable across 400 questions a day.
options.C: The original design: separating the two data fetches lets them run concurrently, which a single call with tools cannot do.
options.D: Neither: this needs an agent, because which data source to consult depends on how the dispatcher phrased the question.

items.question: A health insurer routes member messages into five handler pipelines. About 6% of messages yield a low-confidence classification — mixed-topic messages, or topics outside the taxonomy entirely. The team must decide what happens to them. Which are sound designs for the low-confidence path? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Send them to a general handler with broad retrieval and no narrow persona, and log them as candidate taxonomy gaps.
options.B: Send them to whichever pipeline has the highest prior probability across recent traffic, so members still receive a specialised answer.
options.C: Re-run the classification twice more at temperature and take the majority, since low confidence usually reflects sampling noise.
options.D: Split the low-confidence path by stakes: coverage and claims topics go to a human queue, everything else to the general handler.
options.E: Expand the taxonomy with new categories, adding subtypes, until every message classifies with high confidence.

items.question: An ESG ratings agency publishes company assessments with a fixed nine-section structure mandated by its published methodology. The evidence each section needs varies enormously: one company's emissions section is settled by three disclosures, another's requires a supply-chain investigation across a dozen sources. The current build is a nine-call chain, one call per section, each issuing a fixed retrieval query. Analysts complain that some sections are thin while others cite the same source repeatedly. Which architecture fits?

options.A: Convert the whole assessment to an agent that decides which sections to write and what evidence to gather for each.
options.B: Keep the nine-call chain but give each call a larger fixed retrieval budget, so the thin sections pull in more sources.
options.C: Run the nine section calls concurrently rather than sequentially, with a deduplicating merge across all cited sources.
options.D: Keep the nine sections as fixed workflow steps and make gathering dynamic: a planner issues retrievals into a shared evidence set.

items.question: A semiconductor fab runs a yield-analysis assistant. Today it fans out five fixed workers — process step logs, metrology, equipment maintenance, materials lots, prior excursions — and merges their findings. Which observations would indicate the fixed fan-out should be replaced by an orchestrator that selects workers at runtime? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: The merge step's prompt has grown past 60,000 tokens, and the merge is now the slowest stage of the request.
options.B: The five workers frequently return contradictory readings, which the merge step resolves the wrong way about a third of the time.
options.C: Engineers report that the useful next step depends on the first finding, and the fixed five workers never follow those trails.
options.D: The number of sources genuinely needed ranges from one to more than twenty, and which ones matter cannot be listed in advance.
options.E: Fab engineers want answers in under 30 seconds, and the current five-worker fan-out takes about 45 seconds.

items.question: For which kind of task is prompt chaining the wrong pattern?

options.A: A task whose subtasks each require a different tool, such as a search index for one step and a calculator for another.
options.B: A task whose parts cannot be cleanly separated, because each needs information the others are still producing.
options.C: A task with a strict output schema, since each extra step leaves another place for the format to drift.
options.D: A task in which one subtask is far harder than the rest, since a chain applies the same effort to every step.

items.question: A contact centre deploys real-time agent assist: while the customer is speaking, the system surfaces a suggested next action on the human agent's screen. A suggestion is useful only if it arrives before the agent must reply — the measured window is 2.5 seconds, and later suggestions are ignored or actively distracting. A proposed agentic design is correct on 79% of calls, with a median latency of 1.9 seconds, a p90 of 6 seconds, and 62% of runs completing inside the window. The existing two-step workflow is correct on 68% of calls with a p99 of 1.4 seconds. Which analysis should drive the decision?

options.A: Multiply each design's accuracy by the share of runs inside the 2.5-second window: roughly 49% for the agent against 68%.
options.B: Compare accuracy directly — 79% against 68% — and treat the latency tail as an engineering problem to be optimised after launch.
options.C: Compare median latencies, since the median reflects the typical experience and 1.9 seconds sits comfortably inside the window.
options.D: Deploy the agent and fall back to the workflow's suggestion whenever the agent has not returned inside the 2.5-second window.

items.question: A broadcaster checks machine-generated subtitles against its accessibility standard. The current design is one call per programme that reads the subtitle file alongside the transcript and returns a list of issues. Precision is good, but recall degrades with position: issues in the final third of a two-hour file are missed far more often than issues in the first third. The team has substantial latency headroom and a labelled set of 400 programmes. What should the team do next?

options.A: Move to the highest capability tier and re-measure recall on the 400 labelled programmes before changing the design.
options.B: Add a second pass that re-reads the final third of each subtitle file and merges its issues into the first pass's list.
options.C: Section each programme into overlapping segments checked concurrently with the same prompt, then re-measure recall by position.
options.D: Chain the analysis: summarise the transcript first, then check the subtitle file against that summary instead of the raw text.

items.question: What defines an agent, as distinct from a workflow, in the standard pattern vocabulary?

options.A: It calls tools such as search or code execution, whereas a workflow only chains plain model calls.
options.B: It maintains conversation state and memory across turns, whereas a workflow is stateless between requests.
options.C: It runs on a higher capability tier, such as Opus, because planning its own steps demands stronger reasoning.
options.D: The model directs its own process, choosing the next step and when to stop from environment feedback.

items.question: A telehealth provider summarises consultation notes for onward referral. The notes contain patient identifiers alongside free-text clinical detail. The organisation's data policy permits clinical text to be processed by the model but requires that patient identifiers never appear in a model prompt. The current design sends the whole note in a single call and instructs the model to omit identifiers from its summary. An architect is redesigning. Which decomposition satisfies the policy without degrading summary quality?

options.A: Chain two calls: the first extracts and strips the patient identifiers, the second summarises the clinical text that remains.
options.B: Replace identifiers with placeholders in code before the call, summarise, then substitute the real values back afterwards.
options.C: Keep the single call and add an output guardrail that blocks any summary still containing a recognisable identifier.
options.D: Keep the single call but route notes containing identifiers to a self-hosted model, sending the remainder to Claude.
